title: Projects

content:
This week the main focus of school was integration of an api in a java project. More specifically, requesting a prompt from google gemini and extracting the data from the prompt. Because I already had a feature planned where a user could generate a prompt, containing an idea of something to write about i thought about how i could implement this in atlas.
What I worked on # Integrating gemini API # When i first thought of the “prompt generator” feature, my plan was to have a list of short hard coded prompts in the database, a user could get at random. After learning how to use the gemini API in school, i decided to intergrate that in the feature. So instead of a list of prompts typed manually in the database, I could instead utilize gemini to create unique prompts every time a user asks for one.
This decision automates the feature in atlas, and in concept, would never need to be “updated” by adding new prompts once the user had seen them all, making it fully dynamic. I used the project we made together in school, and when i could sucessully extract a prompt, i made the proper mapper, DTO and DAO classes in order to show the prompt, and for the user to save a prompt they like.
Privacy # A big part of atlas is privacy. I want to ensure that a user can choose whether or not they want their created page to be private or public. Therefore i added an enum to my project called visibility. It contains “PUBLIC” and “PRIVATE”. The reason i choose an enum over a boolean, is that i originally wanted the user to between private, public or a custom setting. The idea with the custom setting was that the user could pick from a list of friends, who they wanted a page to be public with. I quickly decided though, that it was a bit out of scope, and i wanted to focus on basic privacy functionality first. If i decide to add it in the future, the enum makes it easy to add a variant of visibility, which i would not be able to, if i had chosen to use a boolean.
Generic DAO & Custom Methods # What I learned # Testing the Persistence Layer # Creating Reusable Test Data # Testing Entity-Specific Behaviour # Challenges & Problems # Next week #

title: Week 4 — API endpoints & privacy

content:
This week I continued working on Atlas, with a focus on testing the DAO layer.
After creating the basic DAO structure, I wanted to make sure that my database operations worked as expected. I created individual test classes for my DAOs and developed a reusable TestPopulator to provide consistent test data.
I also added custom DAO methods for entities that required functionality beyond the basic CRUD operations provided by my generic DAO.
What I worked on # DAO Testing # I created a separate test class for each DAO so that I could test the functionality of each entity independently.
The tests cover operations such as creating, finding, updating, and deleting entities, as well as custom methods specific to individual DAOs.
This allowed me to test my persistence layer before moving further into the API.
Test Populator # One of the first things I needed was a reliable way of creating test data.
I created a TestPopulator class that persists several instances of each entity into the test database. I considered creating multiple smaller populators, but decided to keep one central populator because many of my entities depend on each other.
For example, a Memory can depend on a Person, Place, Chapter, or AppUser. Having all of the related entities created in one place makes it easier to construct valid test data.
After populating the database, the populator returns a SeededData record containing the persisted entities:
return new SeededData( user1, user2, user3, chapter1, chapter2, chapter3, artifact1, artifact2, artifact3, artifact4, musicType, objectType, vehicleType, fragment1, fragment2, fragment3, entityList1, memory1, memory2, memory3, person1, person2, person3, place1, place2, place3, story1, story2, story3, timeCapsule1, timeCapsule2, timeCapsule3, mention1, mention2, mention3 ); Each test class can then use this data during its setup:
@BeforeEach void setUp() { seeded = TestPopulator.populate(emf); artifactDAO = new ArtifactDAO(emf); } This gives each test a predictable starting point and avoids having to manually create the same test data in every test class.
Generic DAO & Custom Methods # As mentioned in my previous blog post, I moved the basic CRUD operations into an abstract generic DAO class.
The individual DAOs can extend this class and reuse the common functionality instead of implementing the same methods for every entity.
However, I kept the tests as separate classes rather than creating one generic DAO test.
The reason for this is that some of my entities have their own lifecycle methods and additional logic that needs to be tested when entities are created or updated. Because of this, the tests cannot always rely on the exact same behaviour.
For entities with additional functionality, I can therefore add tests specifically for that behaviour.
What I learned # Testing the Persistence Layer # This week gave me a better understanding of why testing the DAO layer is important.
Rather than only checking whether the application works when everything is connected together, I can test the database operations independently.
This makes it easier to identify where a problem occurs. If a test for a DAO fails, I can investigate the persistence logic without having to involve the API or frontend.
Creating Reusable Test Data # I also learned the importance of having a consistent way of creating test data.
Because many of my entities are connected through JPA relationships, creating test data manually inside every test would quickly become repetitive and difficult to maintain.
The TestPopulator gives me one central place where I can define the relationships between my test entities.
Testing Entity-Specific Behaviour # Another thing I learned was that not every DAO can necessarily be treated exactly the same way.
While the generic DAO handles the common CRUD functionality, individual entities can have their own business logic and lifecycle methods.
This means my tests need to cover both the shared DAO functionality and the behaviour that is specific to each entity.
Challenges & Problems # The biggest challenge this week was understanding the dependencies between my entities and creating the correct data needed to test them.
Because many entities have relationships with other entities, I could not simply create one entity in isolation.
For example, when testing an entity that requires an AppUser or another related entity, that related entity needs to exist and be persisted first.
This made the order in which the test data is created important.
It also made me realise that the structure of my test data needs to reflect the same relationships that exist in the actual application.
Next week # Next week I want to continue working towards the Atlas API.
My main focus will be on learning how to expose the functionality I have built through API endpoints and understanding how the different layers of my backend should communicate with each other.
title: Week 3 — Testing the DAO Layer

content:
This week I continued working on Atlas. I focused on the database structure, JPA relationships, and the first steps towards building the API.
I also spent time analysing the entity layer I had created previously and used it as the foundation for developing my DAOs.
What I worked on # Database & DAOs # I started working on the database layer of Atlas by looking at how my entities should interact with the database.
Based on the entity structure, I began developing DAOs (Data Access Objects) for handling database operations.
This helped me understand how the entity layer, JPA, Hibernate, and the database work together.
I also started working with relationships between entities using JPA annotations such as:
@OneToMany @OneToOne @ManyToOne These relationships allow the different parts of Atlas to be connected in the database.
Generics # In order to avoid having the same crud methods written in each DAO class, i created an abstract DAO class the extends my IDAO. Thern each DAO can extend the generic DAO in order to inherit all basic crud methods. This makes my dao classes clean as they only need their custom dao methods in the body.
i also made a generic entity “LinkableEntity”. This was a choice i took especially because of my entityList entity. Which is a feature that allows the user to make a custom list with any entity in the program that can be linked to each other. With a generic entity, the process becomes much smoother.
Annotations & Lombok # I learned more about Java annotations and how they can provide additional information to the application and influence how entities are handled by JPA and Hibernate.
I also worked with Lombok, which helped reduce the amount of boilerplate code in my entity classes.
Instead of manually writing getters, setters, constructors, and other common methods, Lombok can generate them automatically using annotations.
This made my entity classes considerably shorter and easier to maintain.
Entity Lifecycle Methods # While working on my entities, I came across two annotations that I found particularly useful: @PrePersist and @PreUpdate.
@PrePersist allows a method to run automatically before an entity is persisted to the database.
I used it to set default values for fields such as createdAt:
@PrePersist public void setDefaultDate() { if (this.createdAt == null) { this.createdAt = LocalDate.now(); } } This means I don’t have to manually set the creation date every time I create a new entity.
I also worked with @PreUpdate, which runs automatically before an existing entity is updated.
In my entities, I used it to update the updatedAt field and recalculate values such as the word count:
@PreUpdate protected void onUpdate() { updatedAt = LocalDate.now(); calculateWordCount(); } This allows certain values to be updated automatically whenever the entity changes.
What I learned # JPA Relationships # I gained a much better understanding of how entities communicate with each other through JPA relationships.
Previously, I mainly understood entities as individual classes representing database tables. Working with relationships helped me understand how these entities can instead be connected and how those connections are represented in Java.
I learned how annotations such as @OneToMany, @OneToOne, and @ManyToOne can be used to define these relationships.
For example, a user can have multiple memories, while each memory belongs to a specific user.
DAOs # I also gained a better understanding of the purpose of DAOs.
Rather than having database operations directly inside my entities or other parts of the application, the DAO provides a separate place for handling persistence-related operations.
This gave me a clearer idea of how the different layers of my backend can be separated.
Entity Lifecycle # Working with @PrePersist and @PreUpdate also helped me understand that JPA provides ways to react to different stages of an entity’s lifecycle.
This can be useful for automatically handling values such as creation dates, update dates, calculated fields, and other values that should be maintained by the application.
Challenges & Problems # One of the things I had to get used to this week was understanding how the different parts of the backend fit together.
The entity classes, JPA relationships, DAOs, Hibernate, and database are all connected, but each has a different responsibility.
Working through this helped me understand that the backend is not just about creating entities, but about creating a structure where the different layers work together.
Next week # Next week I want to continue building the Atlas API.
My main focus will be on understanding how to expose my backend functionality through API endpoints and continue developing the structure that will eventually allow the React frontend to communicate with the Java backend.
title: Week 2 — Database & Relations

content:
Project Overview # Atlas is a personal journal application designed to help users document, organize, and preserve the important parts of their lives.
The idea is to create a private, personal space where memories, people, places, stories, and meaningful objects can be collected and connected — almost like a personal Wikipedia for your own life.
The project is being developed as a full-stack application, with a Java backend API serving as the foundation and a React frontend providing the user interface.
Project Information # Developer - Andreas Jensen Education - Datamatiker — 3rd semester School - EK Year - 2026 Status - In development Type - Full Stack Application
Goal # The goal of the project is to develop a production-oriented backend that demonstrates the principles and technologies covered throughout the semester.
The backend will include:
User authentication and validation Role-based access control Secure user-specific data CRUD functionality Business rules and data validation JPA and Hibernate persistence PostgreSQL database integration REST API endpoints DTOs for communication between the backend and frontend External API integrations A structure that can be expanded with additional functionality in the future The Idea Behind Atlas # Atlas is built around the idea of preserving your personal story.
Instead of treating memories as isolated diary entries, the application allows different parts of a person’s life to be connected.
For example, a memory about a trip to Italy could be connected to:
The people who were there The places that were visited Photos and other artifacts Related memories A larger chapter of the user’s life This creates a more interconnected way of documenting life rather than simply writing individual journal entries.
Architecture # The project is divided into two main parts:
Backend # The backend is being developed in Java and provides the API and business logic for Atlas.
The current backend stack includes:
Java JPA Hibernate PostgreSQL The backend is responsible for handling persistence, relationships between entities, validation, authentication, and communication with the frontend.
Frontend # The frontend is being developed with React.
It will provide the visual interface through which users can create, view, edit, and organize their personal content.
The frontend will communicate with the Java backend through the REST API.
Core Concepts # Atlas is built around several central concepts:
Chapters Larger periods or phases of a person’s life.
Memories Individual moments or experiences that the user wants to preserve.
People People who are connected to memories, chapters, or other parts of the user’s story.
Places Locations that have significance to the user’s life.
Artifacts Objects or pieces of media that carry personal meaning, such as albums, films, or other meaningful objects.
Entity Lists Custom collections that allow users to organize related items, such as favourite movies, quotes, books, or memories.
Development # Atlas is currently in development as part of my 3rd-semester Datamatiker project at EK.
The project is being developed incrementally, beginning with the backend architecture, database model, and persistence layer before connecting the API to the React frontend.
The long-term goal is to create a polished full-stack application that demonstrates both the technical concepts learned during the semester and a practical, user-focused product.
Technologies # Backend # Java JPA Hibernate PostgreSQL Frontend # React JavaScript HTML CSS Development # IntelliJ IDEA pgAdmin Git / GitHub
